medium.a: P: problems solvable in polynomial time. NP: problems verifiable in polynomial time. P=NP would mean every problem whose solution can be quickly checked can also be quickly solved. This would break all current cryptography and enable efficient solutions to currently intractable problems.
medium.hint: If P=NP, internet encryption (RSA) would be breakable.

medium.q: What is a Turing machine and what does the halting problem prove?
medium.a: A Turing machine is a theoretical computer model. The halting problem asks if a program will halt or run forever β€” Turing proved this is undecidable (no general algorithm exists). It established fundamental limits on computation.
medium.hint: Some problems cannot be solved by any algorithm, regardless of computing power.

medium.q: What is Kolmogorov complexity?
medium.a: Kolmogorov complexity of a string is the length of the shortest computer program that produces that string. It formalises the concept of the 'complexity' of information β€” random strings have high Kolmogorov complexity; structured strings have low complexity.
medium.hint: The shortest description of a random number is the number itself.

medium.q: What is the relationship between Shannon entropy and Kolmogorov complexity?
medium.a: Shannon entropy measures the average information content of a probability distribution. Kolmogorov complexity measures the minimal description length of a specific string. They are related but different: Shannon is probabilistic and statistical; Kolmogorov is deterministic and applies to individual strings.
medium.hint: Both measure 'compressibility' β€” but in different frameworks.

medium.q: What are the Millennium Prize Problems and how many have been solved?
medium.a: Seven unsolved mathematics problems with $1 million prizes. One has been solved: the PoincarΓ© Conjecture (Perelman, 2003 β€” he declined the prize). The other six (Riemann Hypothesis, P vs NP, Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer, Navier-Stokes, Yang-Mills, Hodge Conjecture) remain open.
medium.hint: Six unsolved Millennium Prize Problems remain β€” each worth $1 million.

medium.q: What is the PoincarΓ© conjecture and how was it proved?
medium.a: The PoincarΓ© conjecture stated that every simply connected, closed 3-manifold is homeomorphic to a 3-sphere. Perelman proved it (2003) using Ricci flow with surgery β€” a radically novel approach. It was the only Millennium Problem solved to date.
medium.hint: Simply connected means no holes. Perelman's proof settled a 100-year-old question.

medium.q: What is non-standard analysis and how does it relate to infinitesimals?
medium.a: Non-standard analysis (Robinson) rigorously justifies infinitesimals using hyperreal numbers β€” infinitely small (but non-zero) quantities. Newton and Leibniz used infinitesimals intuitively; standard analysis replaced them with limits; non-standard analysis vindicates their original approach rigorously.
medium.hint: Infinitesimals: quantities smaller than any real positive number but not zero.

hard.q: What is the Langlands Program and why is it considered a 'grand unified theory' of mathematics?
hard.a: The Langlands Program is a vast set of conjectured connections between number theory, automorphic forms, and representation theory. Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem used Langlands connections. If fully realised, it would unify most of mathematics under a single framework.
hard.hint: It connects areas of mathematics that seem unrelated β€” like finding a single language for all mathematics.

hard.q: What is the significance of the Grothendieck's theory of schemes in modern algebraic geometry?
hard.a: Grothendieck revolutionised algebraic geometry by extending it to include all commutative rings as 'geometric spaces' (schemes). This immense generalisation unified seemingly different fields and made possible proofs of deep results (Weil conjectures). It is considered the most ambitious reformulation of mathematics in the 20th century.
hard.hint: Grothendieck made geometry so general it included number theory.

hard.q: What is the abc conjecture and why is its claimed proof controversial?
hard.a: The abc conjecture relates the sum of two coprime integers (a+b=c) to the prime factors of a, b, and c. Shinichi Mochizuki claimed proof in 2012 using a new theory (inter-universal TeichmΓΌller theory), but the proof is so novel that the mathematical community has largely been unable to verify it.
hard.hint: A proof that cannot be understood or verified remains unaccepted.

hard.q: What is non-Euclidean geometry and why did its discovery transform mathematics and physics?
hard.a: Lobachevsky and Bolyai developed hyperbolic geometry where parallel lines can diverge and triangle angles sum to less than 180Β°. Riemann developed spherical geometry. This shattered the belief that Euclidean geometry was the unique description of space, preparing the way for Einstein's general relativity, which uses curved Riemannian spacetime.
hard.hint: Before non-Euclidean geometry, mathematicians believed there was only one possible geometry.

hard.q: What is category theory and why do some mathematicians consider it a foundation for mathematics?
hard.a: Category theory studies mathematical structures and the maps (morphisms) between them, abstracting away from specific objects to study structure-preserving maps. Some mathematicians argue it is a more natural foundation than set theory because it emphasises relationships rather than objects.
hard.hint: If set theory is about what things are, category theory is about how things relate.

hard.q: What is the relationship between complex analysis and the distribution of prime numbers (Riemann Hypothesis)?
hard.a: The Riemann zeta function Ξ¶(s) = Ξ£ 1/nΛΆ can be analytically continued to the complex plane. The distribution of primes is related to the zeros of Ξ¶(s). The Riemann Hypothesis proposes all non-trivial zeros lie on the line Re(s)=1/2 β€” which would prove precise results about prime distribution.
hard.hint: Primes and complex analysis are secretly connected through the zeta function.

hard.q: What is the significance of Galois theory for polynomial equations?
hard.a: Galois theory explains why polynomial equations above degree 4 cannot generally be solved by radicals. It uses group theory (the Galois group of a polynomial's roots) to determine solvability. It unified field theory and group theory, showing abstract algebra determines what calculations are possible.
hard.hint: Galois showed that equations are not solvable by radicals if their symmetry group is too complex.

hard.q: What is topology and what is the hairy ball theorem?
hard.a: Topology studies properties preserved under continuous deformation. The hairy ball theorem states that you cannot comb a hairy ball flat without a cowlick β€” formally, there is no non-vanishing continuous tangent vector field on a sphere. This has applications in physics (magnetic monopoles) and meteorology.
hard.hint: You can't comb a sphere smoothly without a point where the comb can't go β€” that's the hairy ball theorem.

hard.q: What is the concept of 'p-adic numbers' and how do they differ from real numbers?
hard.a: P-adic numbers are an alternative completion of the rationals using a different notion of 'closeness': two numbers are close if their difference is divisible by a high power of prime p. They have a strange geometry (every triangle is isosceles) and are crucial in modern number theory and cryptography.
hard.hint: The 'closeness' in p-adic numbers is about divisibility by p, not about distance on a number line.

hard.q: What is a Lie group and why is it important in physics?
hard.a: A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold β€” combining algebraic and geometric structure. Lie groups describe continuous symmetries of physical systems. The Standard Model of particle physics is formulated using symmetry groups SU(3)Γ—SU(2)Γ—U(1) β€” all Lie groups.
hard.hint: The mathematical description of symmetry in particle physics is Lie group theory.

hard.q: What is the significance of Banach and Hilbert spaces for functional analysis and quantum mechanics?
hard.a: Banach spaces are complete normed vector spaces; Hilbert spaces are Banach spaces with an inner product. Quantum mechanics is formulated in Hilbert space: physical states are vectors; observables are operators; measurements are eigenvalues. Functional analysis provides the rigorous mathematical framework for quantum theory.
hard.hint: Quantum states live in Hilbert space β€” the mathematics of infinite-dimensional vector spaces.

hard.q: What is the Atiyah-Singer Index Theorem and why is it remarkable?
hard.a: The Atiyah-Singer theorem relates the analytical index (related to differential equations) and the topological index (related to the shape of the manifold) of an elliptic operator β€” showing that a purely analytic quantity equals a purely topological one. It unifies analysis, geometry, and topology.
hard.hint: It says the number of solutions to a differential equation is determined by the topology of the space.

hard.q: What is the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture and why does it matter?
hard.a: The BSD conjecture predicts that the number of rational points on an elliptic curve (over Q) equals the order of the zero of the associated L-function at s=1. Unsolved β€” its proof would give an algorithm for finding all rational solutions to elliptic curves, with implications for cryptography and Diophantine geometry.
hard.hint: How many rational solutions does a cubic curve have? BSD says the answer is encoded in a complex function.

hard.q: What is the Yang-Mills existence and mass gap problem?
hard.a: Yang-Mills theory describes fundamental forces using gauge fields. The existence problem asks whether Yang-Mills theory in 4D has rigorous mathematical foundations (not yet formally established). The mass gap problem asks why all particles must have positive mass. Solving either would require new mathematics.
hard.hint: The mathematical physics of the Standard Model requires a rigorous mathematical foundation that doesn't yet exist.

hard.q: What is a modular form and why is it important in number theory?
hard.a: A modular form is a complex analytic function satisfying specific transformation properties under the modular group. They are central to the proof of Fermat's Last Theorem (Wiles linked elliptic curves to modular forms via Taniyama-Shimura), and appear throughout modern number theory.
hard.hint: Every elliptic curve is associated with a modular form β€” this was the key to Fermat.

hard.q: What is the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem?
hard.a: The Navier-Stokes equations describe fluid dynamics. The millennium problem asks: given smooth initial conditions, do solutions always exist and remain smooth for all time, or can singularities (infinitely sharp gradients) develop? Solving this would transform fluid mechanics and turbulence theory.
hard.hint: Turbulence remains poorly understood because we don't know if Navier-Stokes equations always have smooth solutions.

hard.q: What is 'forcing' in set theory and what did Paul Cohen prove?
hard.a: Paul Cohen invented forcing to prove that the Continuum Hypothesis (CH: no set has cardinality strictly between β„µβ‚€ and β„µβ‚) is independent of ZFC set theory. With GΓ¶del's earlier work, this showed CH can neither be proved nor disproved from standard axioms β€” mathematics itself has undecidable propositions.
hard.hint: Cohen showed you can neither prove nor disprove the Continuum Hypothesis from the usual axioms.

hard.q: What is an inaccessible cardinal and why do large cardinals extend the foundations of set theory?
hard.a: Inaccessible cardinals are infinite cardinals too large to be 'reached' from below by standard set operations. They cannot be proved to exist from ZFC axioms β€” their existence is an additional axiom. Large cardinal axioms extend what can be proved, revealing how the consistency of mathematics depends on what infinity we assume.
hard.hint: Some mathematical truths require assuming very large infinities to prove.

hard.q: What is the relationship between decidability, computability, and formal axiom systems?
hard.a: Turing showed some decision problems are undecidable (no algorithm exists). GΓ¶del showed formal systems cannot prove all truths. Together they establish that mathematical truth exceeds what any fixed formal system or algorithm can capture β€” mathematics is irreducibly incomplete.
hard.hint: Truth, provability, and computability are fundamentally different concepts.

hard.q: What is the importance of the Prime Number Theorem and how is it proved?
hard.a: The PNT: Ο€(x) ~ x/ln(x) β€” the number of primes up to x is approximately x/ln(x). Proved by Hadamard and de la VallΓ©e-Poussin (1896) using complex analysis of the Riemann zeta function β€” the first major result connecting primes to complex analysis.
hard.hint: The distribution of primes is predicted by a formula involving logarithms β€” proved using complex numbers.

hard.q: What is the 'curse of dimensionality' in mathematics and machine learning?
hard.a: In high dimensions, volume concentrates near the surface; data points become exponentially farther apart; intuitions from 2D/3D fail. In machine learning, high-dimensional data requires exponentially more training examples to generalise well. Most successful deep learning techniques involve dimension reduction.
hard.hint: In 100 dimensions, most of the volume of a sphere is near its surface.

hard.q: What is the relationship between abstract algebra (groups, rings, fields) and classical number theory?
hard.a: Number theory studies integers and primes; abstract algebra provides the structural framework to understand them. The integers form a ring; modular arithmetic creates quotient rings; prime factorisation generalises to unique factorisation domains; Galois groups explain which equations are solvable. Abstract algebra translates number-theoretic questions into structural ones.
hard.hint: The deep results in number theory (Fermat, quadratic reciprocity, Galois theory) all use abstract algebraic structures.

hard.q: What is the Hodge conjecture and why is it important?
hard.a: The Hodge conjecture asks whether algebraic cycles (built from polynomial equations) can represent all topological cycles in algebraic geometry. It would unify the algebraic and topological descriptions of complex manifolds. It is one of the remaining six unsolved Millennium Prize Problems.
hard.hint: Can topological information about a space always be captured by algebraic equations?

hard.q: What is 'computational complexity theory' and describe the complexity classes P, NP, NP-complete, and NP-hard?
hard.a: P: decidable in polynomial time. NP: verifiable in polynomial time. NP-complete: in NP and every NP problem reduces to it (SAT is NP-complete). NP-hard: at least as hard as NP-complete problems (may not be in NP). If P=NP, then NP=NP-complete=P.
hard.hint: Complexity classes describe inherent difficulty of problems, independent of computational technology.

hard.q: What is an ultrafilter and how is it used in non-standard analysis?
hard.a: An ultrafilter on β„• is a maximal filter β€” for every subset A of β„•, either A or its complement is in the filter. Robinson used ultrafilters to construct hyperreal numbers: sequences of reals are identified if they agree on a set in the ultrafilter. This yields rigorous infinitesimals.
hard.hint: Ultrafilters allow you to consistently say that almost all of a sequence does something.

hard.q: What is the significance of Andrew Wiles's proof of Fermat's Last Theorem?
hard.a: Wiles's 1995 proof was the culmination of 358 years of attempts. It linked elliptic curves to modular forms (Taniyama-Shimura conjecture), required new techniques (Galois representations, Iwasawa theory, Euler systems). Beyond FLT, the methods themselves revolutionised number theory.
hard.hint: Proving FLT required creating new mathematics β€” the tools didn't exist before Wiles.

hard.q: What is abstract algebra's role in cryptography?
hard.a: Modern cryptography (RSA, Diffie-Hellman, elliptic curve cryptography) is built on algebraic structures: integer arithmetic modulo n (RSA), cyclic groups (Diffie-Hellman), and elliptic curves over finite fields (ECC). Security rests on computationally hard problems: factoring large integers, discrete logarithm problem.
hard.hint: The difficulty of factoring a 2048-bit number is what keeps your bank details safe.

hard.q: What is the relationship between topology and data analysis (TDA β€” Topological Data Analysis)?
hard.a: TDA applies topological tools (persistent homology) to analyse the 'shape' of high-dimensional data. It identifies features (clusters, loops, voids) that persist across scales and are robust to noise. Applications: cancer cell shape analysis, materials science, brain network analysis.
hard.hint: Topology gives tools to detect 'shape' in data that statistical methods miss.

hard.q: What is the relationship between information theory, thermodynamics, and statistical mechanics?
hard.a: Shannon's entropy formula is mathematically identical to Boltzmann's thermodynamic entropy formula. Maxwell's demon thought experiment links information erasure to thermodynamic cost (Landauer's principle: erasing one bit produces kTΒ·ln(2) heat). Information and physics are deeply connected at a fundamental level.
hard.hint: Deleting information generates heat β€” information has physical consequences.

hard.q: What is the significance of the Yang-Baxter equation in mathematical physics?
hard.a: The Yang-Baxter equation expresses a consistency condition for scattering matrices in quantum mechanics and integrable systems. Its solutions (R-matrices) parametrise integrable models in 2D and quantum groups. It connects statistical mechanics, knot theory, and quantum groups.
hard.hint: The same equation appears in quantum mechanics, knot theory, and statistical physics β€” revealing unexpected connections.

hard.q: What is the Collatz conjecture and why does it resist proof despite its simple statement?
hard.a: The Collatz conjecture: starting from any positive integer, if even divide by 2; if odd multiply by 3 and add 1. Conjecture: always reach 1 eventually. Verified for vast numbers but unproven. It resists proof because the sequence's behaviour is effectively random, and no algebraic structure exploitable by standard techniques has been found.
hard.hint: The simplest unsolved problem in mathematics β€” or one of them.

easy.q: What is a superconductor?
easy.a: A material that conducts electricity with zero resistance below a critical temperature, allowing current to flow indefinitely without energy loss
easy.hint: Current applications include MRI machines and particle accelerators.

easy.q: What is quantum tunnelling?
easy.a: The quantum mechanical phenomenon where a particle passes through an energy barrier that it classically shouldn't be able to cross
easy.hint: It's responsible for nuclear fusion in the Sun and is used in tunnel diodes.

easy.q: What is radioactive decay?
easy.a: The spontaneous disintegration of an unstable atomic nucleus, emitting radiation (alpha, beta, gamma) and transforming into a more stable nucleus
easy.hint: It is random at the individual atom level β€” only populations follow predictable decay curves.

easy.q: What is a neutrino?
easy.a: A nearly massless, chargeless elementary particle that interacts only via the weak force and gravity, able to pass through ordinary matter almost undetected
easy.hint: Trillions of neutrinos from the Sun pass through your body every second.

easy.q: What is dark matter?
easy.a: A hypothetical form of matter that does not interact with light but has gravitational effects. It accounts for ~27% of the universe's mass-energy, evidenced by galaxy rotation curves and gravitational lensing.
easy.hint: We know it's there because of its gravity β€” but we've never detected it directly.

easy.q: What is the Standard Model of particle physics?
easy.a: The theoretical framework describing the fundamental particles (quarks, leptons) and three of the four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, weak, strong) via force-carrying bosons
easy.hint: It does not include gravity β€” that's general relativity's domain.

easy.q: What is antimatter?
easy.a: Matter composed of antiparticles: for every particle, there is a corresponding antiparticle with opposite charge. When matter meets antimatter, they annihilate, releasing energy (E=mcΒ²).
easy.hint: The universe appears to have more matter than antimatter β€” one of physics' great unsolved mysteries.

easy.q: What is SchrΓ¶dinger's cat thought experiment?
easy.a: A thought experiment showing the paradox of applying quantum superposition to macroscopic objects: a cat in a box is simultaneously 'alive' and 'dead' until observed, illustrating the measurement problem in quantum mechanics.
easy.hint: It's absurd β€” which is the point. Quantum mechanics seems absurd at macroscopic scales.

easy.q: What is the photoelectric effect and what did Einstein explain about it?
easy.a: When light hits a metal surface, electrons are ejected only if the light exceeds a threshold frequency. Einstein explained that light consists of photons with energy E=hf β€” proving light's particle nature and earning his Nobel Prize.
easy.hint: This cannot be explained by wave theory β€” only particle theory works.

easy.q: What is the wave-particle duality of matter?
easy.a: All quantum objects exhibit both wave and particle behaviour, depending on the experiment. de Broglie proposed particles have wavelength Ξ»=h/p. This explains electron diffraction and is the foundation of quantum mechanics.
easy.hint: Electrons produce interference patterns β€” a wave phenomenon β€” yet also hit screens at single points β€” a particle phenomenon.

easy.q: What is a semiconductor?
easy.a: A material with electrical conductivity between a conductor and an insulator, controllable by temperature, doping, or light. Silicon semiconductors are the basis of all modern electronics.
easy.hint: The transistor (in every computer chip) is a semiconductor device.

easy.q: What is Moore's Law?
easy.a: The observation by Gordon Moore (1965) that the number of transistors in an integrated circuit doubles approximately every two years, leading to exponential growth in computing power. It has largely held for decades but is now approaching physical limits.
easy.hint: Transistors are now a few atoms wide β€” there isn't much further to shrink.

easy.q: What is CRISPR-Cas9 and why is it a major scientific breakthrough?
easy.a: CRISPR-Cas9 is a precise gene-editing tool using guide RNA to direct the Cas9 protein to cut specific DNA sequences. It has dramatically reduced the cost and difficulty of genetic engineering, enabling new medical treatments, crop improvements, and research.
easy.hint: It's like molecular scissors that can cut DNA at any location you choose.

easy.q: What is stem cell therapy?
easy.a: The use of stem cells (undifferentiated cells capable of becoming many cell types) to treat diseases by replacing damaged or defective cells. Applications include treating leukaemia, spinal injuries, and potentially Parkinson's and diabetes.
easy.hint: Stem cells can become whatever type of cell the body needs.

easy.q: What is epigenetics?
easy.a: The study of heritable changes in gene expression that do not involve changes to the DNA sequence β€” caused by methylation, histone modification, etc. Environmental factors can alter epigenetic marks, affecting which genes are active.
easy.hint: The same DNA can be expressed differently β€” epigenetics explains how.

easy.q: What is a black hole?
easy.a: A region of spacetime where gravity is so extreme that nothing, not even light, can escape beyond the event horizon. Formed by collapsed massive stars or at the centres of galaxies.
easy.hint: Stephen Hawking showed black holes slowly evaporate via Hawking radiation.

easy.q: What is dark energy?
easy.a: A hypothetical form of energy accounting for ~68% of the universe's mass-energy, responsible for the observed accelerating expansion of the universe. Its nature is unknown.
easy.hint: Dark energy acts like an anti-gravity force pushing the universe apart.

easy.q: What is the Big Bang theory?
easy.a: The cosmological model proposing that the universe began ~13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense state and has been expanding and cooling ever since
easy.hint: Evidence: cosmic microwave background radiation, Hubble's observation of galaxy recession, element abundances.

easy.q: What is Hawking radiation?
easy.a: Radiation theoretically predicted by Stephen Hawking to be emitted by black holes due to quantum effects near the event horizon, causing black holes to slowly evaporate over extremely long time periods
easy.hint: It suggests black holes are not permanent β€” they slowly 'evaporate.'

easy.q: What is the cosmic microwave background?
easy.a: The thermal radiation left over from the early universe (~380,000 years after the Big Bang) when the universe cooled enough for atoms to form. It is observed as a uniform ~2.7 K glow in every direction.
easy.hint: It is the 'baby photo' of the universe.

easy.q: What is a pulsar?
easy.a: A rapidly rotating neutron star that emits beams of electromagnetic radiation. The rotation causes the beams to sweep past Earth regularly, appearing as pulses.
easy.hint: When pulsars were first discovered, astronomers briefly thought they might be alien signals.

easy.q: What is string theory?
easy.a: A theoretical physics framework proposing that elementary particles are not points but one-dimensional 'strings' vibrating at different frequencies. It is a candidate for a 'theory of everything' but has not been experimentally verified.
easy.hint: Different string vibrations produce different particles β€” like a musical instrument producing different notes.

easy.q: What is the concept of 'emergent phenomena' and give an example from condensed matter physics?
easy.a: Emergent phenomena are properties of systems that cannot be predicted from individual components. Example: superconductivity β€” individual electrons resist flow, but below a critical temperature, Cooper pairs form and conduct with zero resistance.
easy.hint: The whole behaves in ways the parts don't.

easy.q: What is the Higgs boson?
easy.a: The particle associated with the Higgs field, which gives elementary particles their mass. Discovered at CERN's LHC in 2012, it completed the Standard Model of particle physics.
easy.hint: Without the Higgs field, particles would have no mass and travel at light speed.

easy.q: What is nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) and what is it used for?
easy.a: NMR is the response of certain atomic nuclei to radio waves in a magnetic field. Used in MRI (medical imaging) and chemical structure analysis. The resonance frequency depends on the atomic environment.
easy.hint: Your MRI scan uses nuclear magnetic resonance β€” the 'nuclear' is often dropped for public relations reasons.

easy.q: What is the difference between a type I and type II superconductor?
easy.a: Type I: becomes superconducting below a single critical field strength; completely expels magnetic fields (Meissner effect). Type II: has two critical fields; between them, magnetic flux penetrates in quantised vortices. Type II includes most practical superconductors.
easy.hint: Type II superconductors are used in MRI magnets because they tolerate higher magnetic fields.

easy.q: What is holography in physics?
easy.a: A technique for recording and reconstructing three-dimensional images using laser interference patterns. The holographic principle in theoretical physics proposes that the information content of a volume of space is encoded on its boundary surface.
easy.hint: The holographic principle suggests our 3D universe may be encoded on a 2D surface.

easy.q: What is quantum computing?
easy.a: A computing paradigm using quantum bits (qubits) that can exist in superpositions of 0 and 1 simultaneously. This allows certain calculations (factoring, searching, simulating quantum systems) to be performed exponentially faster than classical computers.
easy.hint: Quantum computers don't replace classical computers β€” they solve a different set of problems faster.

easy.q: What is bioluminescence and what organisms use it?
easy.a: Bioluminescence is the production and emission of light by living organisms through chemical reactions (typically luciferin + luciferase + Oβ‚‚). Organisms: fireflies, deep-sea fish, some jellyfish, squid, and certain bacteria.
easy.hint: Deep sea environments where sunlight doesn't reach are full of bioluminescent organisms.

easy.q: What is the endosymbiosis theory and what evidence supports it?
easy.a: Lynn Margulis proposed mitochondria and chloroplasts were once free-living bacteria that were engulfed by early eukaryotic cells. Evidence: they have their own circular DNA, are similar in size to bacteria, have double membranes, and reproduce by binary fission.
easy.hint: Your mitochondria were once independent organisms.

easy.q: What is systems biology?
easy.a: The study of biological systems as integrated, complex networks of interacting components, using mathematical modelling and computation to understand emergent properties that cannot be explained by studying individual components
easy.hint: Systems biology looks at networks of genes, proteins, and metabolites as a whole.

easy.q: What is 'convergent evolution' and why does it occur?
easy.a: Independent evolution of similar traits in unrelated lineages in response to similar environmental pressures. Examples: wings in birds, bats, insects; eyes in vertebrates and cephalopods; streamlined body shapes in dolphins, sharks, and ichthyosaurs.
easy.hint: Natural selection finds similar solutions to similar problems, regardless of ancestry.

easy.q: What is directed evolution and what was the 2018 Nobel Prize for?
easy.a: Directed evolution uses mutation and selection in the lab to engineer proteins with desired properties. Frances Arnold won the 2018 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing directed evolution of enzymes β€” creating highly efficient industrial enzymes impossible to design rationally.
easy.hint: Darwin's mechanism of evolution applied in the laboratory.

easy.q: What is synthetic biology and give an application?
easy.a: Synthetic biology designs and constructs new biological parts and systems. Applications: engineering bacteria to produce insulin, biofuels, or medicines; creating logic circuits in cells; programmable therapeutics targeting cancer.
easy.hint: Biology as engineering β€” life as a design problem.

easy.q: What is the concept of 'metabolic engineering'?
easy.a: Modifying a cell's metabolic pathways to produce desired compounds (drugs, biofuels, materials). Yeast have been engineered to produce opioids, cannabinoids, artemisinin (anti-malarial), and various industrial chemicals.
easy.hint: Reprogramming a cell's biochemistry to produce useful products.

easy.q: What is CRISPR base editing?
easy.a: A CRISPR variant that changes individual DNA bases (A to G, C to T) without cutting the double helix β€” allowing precise corrections to point mutations that cause genetic diseases, with fewer off-target effects than standard CRISPR-Cas9.
easy.hint: More precise than cutting β€” a 'pencil edit' rather than 'cut and paste.'

easy.q: What is a photovoltaic cell?
easy.a: A device that converts light energy directly into electrical energy using the photoelectric effect in a semiconductor material (usually silicon). Multiple cells form a solar panel.
easy.hint: Solar panels are made of photovoltaic cells.

easy.q: What is the 'many worlds interpretation' of quantum mechanics?
easy.a: Hugh Everett's interpretation: every quantum measurement causes the universe to branch into multiple worlds, one for each possible outcome. No collapse of the wavefunction occurs β€” all outcomes are realised in parallel universes.
easy.hint: Instead of the wavefunction collapsing, the universe splits.

easy.q: What is the photoelectric effect and what applications does it have?
easy.a: When photons above a threshold frequency hit a surface, they eject electrons (photoelectric effect). Applications: solar cells, photomultiplier tubes, image sensors (CCD cameras), night vision devices, and photodetectors.
easy.hint: Without the photoelectric effect, there would be no solar power.

easy.q: What is a Bose-Einstein condensate?
easy.a: A state of matter formed when bosons are cooled to near absolute zero β€” they lose individual identities and occupy the same quantum state, behaving as a single quantum entity. First created in 1995 (Cornell, Wieman, Ketterle β€” Nobel 2001).
easy.hint: A fifth state of matter where quantum effects become macroscopically visible.

easy.q: What is the Pauli exclusion principle?
easy.a: No two identical fermions (particles with half-integer spin, like electrons) can simultaneously occupy the same quantum state. This explains atomic structure (electrons fill different orbitals) and the stability of matter.
easy.hint: Without the Pauli principle, all electrons would fall into the lowest energy level and chemistry would not exist.

easy.q: What is quasiparticle theory?
easy.a: In condensed matter physics, quasiparticles are collective excitations of a many-body system that behave like particles. Examples: phonons (vibrations in a lattice), magnons (spin waves), Cooper pairs (superconducting). They simplify the description of complex systems.
easy.hint: A sound wave in a crystal acts like a particle (phonon) for quantum mechanical calculations.

easy.q: What is a topological insulator?
easy.a: A material that is an insulator in its bulk but conducts electricity on its surface due to topological properties of its electronic band structure. The surface states are protected by time-reversal symmetry and are robust to impurities.
easy.hint: The surface conducting states cannot be destroyed by small perturbations β€” they are topologically protected.

easy.q: What is the significance of the Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP)?
easy.a: WMAP (2001β€“2010) precisely mapped the cosmic microwave background, determining the universe's age (13.77 billion years), composition (4.9% ordinary matter, 26.8% dark matter, 68.3% dark energy), and confirming the Big Bang theory and inflationary model.
easy.hint: WMAP gave us the most precise measurements of the universe's fundamental parameters.

easy.q: What is exoplanet detection and what methods are used?
easy.a: Exoplanets are planets outside our solar system. Detection methods: transit (planet crosses star, reduces light β€” Kepler); radial velocity (planet's gravity wobbles the star β€” Doppler shift); direct imaging; gravitational microlensing. Over 5,000 exoplanets confirmed to date.
easy.hint: Most exoplanets are detected indirectly β€” by their effects on their star.

easy.q: What is the significance of RNA interference (RNAi)?
easy.a: RNAi is a biological process where small double-stranded RNA molecules silence specific gene expression by degrading complementary mRNA. Discovered by Fire and Mello (Nobel 2006), it has applications in gene therapy and studying gene function.
easy.hint: RNAi is a natural gene-silencing mechanism β€” cells use it to regulate their own genes.

easy.q: What is metagenomics?
easy.a: The study of genetic material recovered directly from environmental samples, without cultivating individual organisms in the lab. It has revealed vast biodiversity of microorganisms that cannot be grown in culture and transformed our understanding of microbial ecosystems.
easy.hint: Most microorganisms in the ocean and soil cannot be grown in a lab β€” metagenomics studies them anyway.

easy.q: What is optogenetics?
easy.a: A technique using light-sensitive proteins (channelrhodopsins) introduced into specific neurons to control their activity with light pulses. It allows precise, cell-type-specific manipulation of neural circuits to study brain function.
easy.hint: Shining light on a neuron to make it fire β€” revolutionised neuroscience.

easy.q: What is proteomics?
easy.a: The large-scale study of all the proteins produced by a cell, tissue, or organism at a given time β€” the 'proteome.' Proteins actually perform biological functions; proteomics supplements genomics by showing what the genes are doing.
easy.hint: You can know the genome but still not know which proteins are present and active.

medium.q: Explain the EPR paradox and Bell's theorem and what they imply about quantum mechanics.
medium.a: EPR (Einstein, Podolsky, Rosen) argued quantum entanglement implied hidden variables must determine particle states β€” preserving locality. Bell's theorem derived testable inequalities that local hidden variable theories must satisfy. Bell test experiments violate these inequalities, proving quantum mechanics is genuinely non-local β€” entanglement is real, not hidden variables.
medium.hint: Nature itself is non-local β€” EPR was wrong, Bell was right.

medium.q: What is the Mach-Zehnder interferometer experiment and what does it demonstrate about quantum superposition?
medium.a: A photon is split at a beam splitter, travels two paths, and recombines. If both paths are open, interference occurs (photon detected at only one exit). If one path is blocked, interference disappears. This demonstrates that the photon existed in superposition, taking both paths simultaneously until measured.
medium.hint: The photon 'knows' whether both paths are open β€” interference requires superposition.

medium.q: What is the renormalization problem in quantum field theory?
medium.a: Quantum field theory calculations often produce infinite answers (due to summing over all possible virtual particle interactions). Renormalization is a systematic procedure to remove these infinities by absorbing them into the physical constants (mass, charge). Feynman, Schwinger, and Tomonaga developed it (Nobel 1965).
medium.hint: Infinities appear when calculating self-energy of particles β€” renormalization makes them finite.

medium.q: What is the quantum Zeno effect?
medium.a: If a quantum system is measured very frequently, its evolution is slowed β€” the watched quantum pot never boils. By repeatedly collapsing the wavefunction, rapid measurement prevents a quantum transition from occurring. It demonstrates how observation itself affects quantum evolution.
medium.hint: Watching a quantum system prevents it from evolving β€” the act of measurement has physical consequences.

medium.q: What is the relationship between entropy and information in Maxwell's demon thought experiment?
medium.a: Maxwell proposed a demon sorting fast/slow molecules could decrease entropy without work. Leo Szilard showed the demon must acquire information about molecules, and Landauer showed erasing that information requires heat (kTΒ·ln2 per bit), resolving the paradox. Information erasure is irreversible and produces entropy.
medium.hint: Deleting information produces heat β€” information is physical.

medium.q: Explain the concept of spontaneous symmetry breaking and its role in particle physics.
medium.a: A system can have symmetric equations but an asymmetric ground state (equilibrium). Example: a ball at the top of a Mexican hat rolls to one side, breaking the rotational symmetry. The Higgs mechanism uses spontaneous symmetry breaking to give W and Z bosons mass while keeping photons massless.
medium.hint: The laws of physics are symmetric, but the universe isn't β€” spontaneous symmetry breaking explains why.

medium.q: What is the significance of the discovery of the Higgs boson for the completeness of the Standard Model?
medium.a: The Higgs boson was the last predicted particle of the Standard Model. Its discovery at CERN's LHC (2012) completed the model and confirmed the Higgs mechanism for mass generation. However, the Standard Model is still incomplete: it doesn't include gravity, dark matter, or explain matter-antimatter asymmetry.
medium.hint: Completing the Standard Model is only a partial victory β€” it leaves major questions unanswered.

medium.q: What is string theory and what problems does it attempt to solve?
medium.a: String theory replaces point particles with one-dimensional vibrating strings. It attempts to unify gravity (general relativity) with quantum mechanics (currently incompatible). It requires 10-11 dimensions; the extra dimensions are compactified. It predicts supersymmetry but has no experimental confirmation.
medium.hint: String theory is mathematically beautiful and may be wrong β€” it's not testable with current technology.

medium.q: What is loop quantum gravity and how does it differ from string theory?
medium.a: Loop quantum gravity (LQG) quantises spacetime itself β€” space has a discrete structure at the Planck scale (~10β»Β³βµ m). Unlike string theory, LQG does not require extra dimensions or supersymmetry. Both are candidates for quantum gravity, but neither has experimental support.
medium.hint: LQG says space is made of discrete quantum loops; string theory says matter is made of vibrating strings.

medium.q: What is holographic duality (AdS/CFT) and what does it suggest about the nature of spacetime?
medium.a: The AdS/CFT correspondence (Maldacena 1997) proposes that a string theory in Anti-de Sitter spacetime is dual to a conformal field theory on its boundary β€” a lower-dimensional description. It suggests spacetime and gravity may be emergent phenomena encoded on a lower-dimensional quantum field theory.
medium.hint: Spacetime gravity in 3D might be fully described by quantum physics on a 2D surface.

medium.q: What is Planck's constant and why is it fundamental to quantum mechanics?
medium.a: Planck's constant h = 6.626 Γ— 10β»Β³β΄ JΒ·s sets the scale of quantum effects. It appears in: E=hf (photon energy); de Broglie wavelength Ξ»=h/p; Heisenberg uncertainty principle Ξ”xΞ”p β‰¥ β„/2. Where hβ†’0, quantum mechanics reduces to classical mechanics.
medium.hint: Planck's constant is how 'quantum' physics is. In a world where h=0, quantum effects vanish.

medium.q: What is the Casimir effect and what does it demonstrate about the quantum vacuum?
medium.a: Two uncharged parallel plates in vacuum attract each other due to quantum vacuum fluctuations β€” virtual particle pairs are excluded between the plates, creating a net inward pressure. This demonstrates that the quantum vacuum is not empty but full of fluctuating fields.
medium.hint: Empty space isn't empty β€” quantum fluctuations have measurable effects.

medium.q: What is superposition versus entanglement in quantum mechanics?
medium.a: Superposition: a single quantum object exists in multiple states simultaneously until measured. Entanglement: two or more quantum objects have correlated quantum states β€” measuring one instantly determines the other's state regardless of distance. Entanglement is a form of non-local correlation stronger than any classical correlation.
medium.hint: Superposition is about one particle; entanglement is about correlations between particles.

medium.q: What is quantum error correction and why is it necessary for quantum computing?
medium.a: Quantum computers are extremely sensitive to noise (decoherence) β€” any interaction with the environment collapses quantum states. Quantum error correction uses redundant encoding of logical qubits in multiple physical qubits to detect and correct errors without measuring (and thus collapsing) the quantum state.
medium.hint: You can't copy a quantum state (no-cloning theorem) β€” error correction must use different methods than classical.

medium.q: What is the significance of the neutrino mass problem for the Standard Model?
medium.a: The Standard Model originally assumed neutrinos were massless. The discovery of neutrino oscillations (Nobel 2015) proved neutrinos have tiny but non-zero masses, requiring extensions to the Standard Model. This also implies a mass generation mechanism (possibly see-saw mechanism) not yet understood.
medium.hint: Neutrino masses are the first confirmed physics beyond the Standard Model.

medium.q: What is an Feynman diagram and what do they calculate?
medium.a: Feynman diagrams are pictorial representations of mathematical terms in the perturbation expansion of quantum field theory. Each diagram corresponds to a quantum process (particle interaction, emission, absorption). Summing all diagrams gives the amplitude for a process, allowing calculation of scattering cross-sections and decay rates.
medium.hint: Each line and vertex in a Feynman diagram corresponds to a specific mathematical expression.

medium.q: What is the concept of symmetry breaking and the Goldstone theorem?
medium.a: When a continuous symmetry is spontaneously broken (system chooses a specific ground state), Goldstone's theorem predicts the emergence of massless bosons (Goldstone bosons). In the electroweak theory, these are 'eaten' by gauge bosons to give them mass (Higgs mechanism).
medium.hint: Breaking continuous symmetry creates massless particles β€” which then give mass to other particles in the Higgs mechanism.

medium.q: What is the quantum Hall effect and why is it topologically protected?
medium.a: In a 2D electron system in a strong magnetic field at low temperature, electrical conductance is quantised in units of eΒ²/h to extraordinary precision. This quantisation is topological β€” it doesn't depend on sample impurities or disorder. It revealed the importance of topology in condensed matter physics.
medium.hint: The quantisation is exact because it is protected by topology, not fine-tuned by physical details.

medium.q: What is the concept of 'emergence' in physics and give three examples.
medium.a: Emergence: properties of complex systems that cannot be predicted from individual components. Examples: superconductivity (individual electrons resist; Cooper pairs conduct with zero resistance); superfluidity (collective quantum fluid behaviour); consciousness (neurons fire, mind emerges). Emergence is ubiquitous in nature.
medium.hint: The whole has properties the parts simply don't have.

medium.q: What is the Penrose-Hawking singularity theorem?
medium.a: Penrose (1965) proved that if a trapped surface (event horizon) exists, a singularity must form inside. Hawking extended this to cosmology: under general relativity, the Big Bang was a singularity. This proved singularities are generic features of general relativity, not mathematical artifacts.
medium.hint: Black hole singularities and the Big Bang are inevitable consequences of general relativity β€” not just theoretical possibilities.

medium.q: What is quantum chromodynamics (QCD) and what is 'colour charge'?
medium.a: QCD is the quantum field theory of the strong nuclear force, describing interactions between quarks via gluons. Quarks carry 'colour charge' (red, green, blue β€” not actual colours). Gluons themselves carry colour charge (unlike photons, which are uncharged), making the strong force self-interacting and highly complex.
medium.hint: Quarks are never found alone β€” QCD's self-coupling confines them inside hadrons.

medium.q: What is the measurement problem in quantum mechanics and what interpretations exist?
medium.a: The measurement problem: the SchrΓ¶dinger equation says superpositions persist, but observation always finds definite outcomes. How does superposition 'collapse' to a definite state? Interpretations: Copenhagen (collapse is postulated); Many Worlds (no collapse, universe branches); pilot wave; relational QM. None is definitively established.
medium.hint: This is one of the deepest unresolved problems in physics and philosophy.

medium.q: What is the Landauer principle and why does it connect computation, information, and thermodynamics?
medium.a: Landauer's principle: erasing one bit of information requires at least kTΒ·ln(2) energy dissipated as heat. This connects logical operations (information processing) to physical thermodynamics. It implies computation is irreversible and has a minimum thermodynamic cost.
medium.hint: Information is physical β€” deleting it produces entropy.

medium.q: What is the hierarchy problem in particle physics?
medium.a: The Higgs boson mass (125 GeV) is vastly smaller than the Planck mass (~10ΒΉβΉ GeV) β€” the natural scale for quantum gravity. Quantum corrections should push it up to the Planck scale. Why it remains small ('naturalness') is the hierarchy problem. Proposed solutions: supersymmetry, extra dimensions, technicolour.
medium.hint: Why is the Higgs boson so much lighter than the Planck scale? This seems like an unnatural fine-tuning.

medium.q: What is the difference between type I, type II, and type III civilisations (Kardashev scale)?
medium.a: The Kardashev scale measures civilisational energy use: Type I uses all energy available on its planet. Type II harnesses all energy from its star (Dyson sphere). Type III harnesses the energy of its entire galaxy. Earth is currently ~Type 0.73.
medium.hint: We are not yet a Type I civilisation β€” we use only a fraction of the energy falling on Earth.

medium.q: What is the origin of elements beyond hydrogen and helium?
medium.a: H and He were produced in Big Bang nucleosynthesis. Heavier elements up to iron were produced in stellar nucleosynthesis (fusion in stars). Elements heavier than iron are produced in neutron star mergers (r-process) and supernovae (s-process). We are literally made of stardust.
medium.hint: Every atom heavier than helium in your body was forged in a star.

medium.q: What is the relationship between thermodynamic entropy and the arrow of time?
medium.a: The second law of thermodynamics (entropy increases) defines a temporal asymmetry β€” past had lower entropy than future. All microscopic physical laws are time-reversible; only the second law distinguishes past from future. The universe started in an extraordinarily low-entropy state (Big Bang), driving entropy increase.
medium.hint: Why does time only run in one direction? The answer is entropy.

medium.q: How does quantum gravity aim to reconcile general relativity and quantum mechanics?
medium.a: General relativity: gravity = curvature of spacetime (continuous). Quantum mechanics: discrete, probabilistic. They are mathematically incompatible at the Planck scale. Quantum gravity attempts to quantise spacetime itself. Candidate theories: string theory, loop quantum gravity. No experimental test yet distinguishes them.
medium.hint: The universe's smallest and largest scales require incompatible theories β€” unifying them is physics' greatest challenge.

hard.q: What is the relationship between gauge symmetry and the fundamental forces in the Standard Model?
hard.a: Each fundamental force arises from invariance under a gauge transformation: electromagnetism from U(1) symmetry, weak force from SU(2), strong force from SU(3). The requirement that physics remains invariant under local gauge transformations necessitates the existence of force-carrying gauge bosons. Gauge symmetry is the deepest structural principle of the Standard Model.
hard.hint: The forces exist because the laws of physics must not change when you change certain mathematical parameters locally.

hard.q: What is the problem of time in quantum gravity?
hard.a: In quantum mechanics, time is a fixed background parameter. In general relativity, time is part of the dynamic spacetime geometry. When you try to combine them (Wheeler-DeWitt equation), time disappears from the equations β€” the 'frozen formalism problem.' This suggests time is not fundamental but emergent from some deeper description.
hard.hint: Time may not be a fundamental feature of reality but an emergent property of something deeper.

hard.q: What is 'naturalness' in particle physics and why has the LHC's failure to find supersymmetry challenged it?
hard.a: Naturalness: fundamental parameters should not require fine-tuning to produce observed values. The Higgs mass seems unnatural (needs tuning to ~30 decimal places to cancel quantum corrections) β€” supersymmetry was the favoured solution. The LHC found no supersymmetric particles, challenging both the naturalness principle and the major theory motivated by it.
hard.hint: If supersymmetry doesn't exist, why is the Higgs mass so unnaturally small?

hard.q: What is the concept of 'the multiverse' and how does it arise from different physical theories?
hard.a: Multiple multiverse types: cosmological inflation predicts eternal inflation creating bubble universes with different physical constants. Many-worlds QM creates branching universes at every quantum measurement. String theory landscape (~10βµβ°β° possible universes). All are untestable with current or foreseeable technology, raising questions about whether they are scientific.
hard.hint: Different physical theories independently arrive at multiverse conclusions β€” but are they all science?

hard.q: What is Hawking radiation and what does it imply about the information paradox?
hard.a: Hawking showed that quantum effects near an event horizon cause black holes to emit thermal radiation, slowly evaporating. The information paradox: if the radiation is truly thermal (random), information about matter that fell in is lost β€” violating quantum mechanics' unitarity (information is conserved). Whether information is destroyed or preserved (encoded in the radiation) is unresolved.
hard.hint: If black holes destroy information, they would violate quantum mechanics β€” one of the deepest puzzles in physics.

hard.q: What is the concept of 'emergence' versus 'reduction' in physics and give examples?
hard.a: Reductionism: complex phenomena can be fully explained by their components. Emergence: new properties arise that cannot be predicted from components. Debate: is thermodynamics fully reducible to statistical mechanics? Is consciousness fully reducible to neuroscience? Even in physics, emergent phenomena (superconductivity, turbulence) resist full reductionist treatment.
hard.hint: Can you predict wetness from the quantum mechanics of hydrogen and oxygen? Or does wetness 'emerge'?

hard.q: What is the significance of the 'amplituhedron' in quantum field theory?
hard.a: The amplituhedron is a geometric object whose volume directly gives the probability of quantum particle interactions, without the need for Feynman diagrams. It suggests that space, time, and quantum mechanics are not fundamental β€” they emerge from deeper geometric principles. It represents a potential reformulation of physics.
hard.hint: A geometric shape that encodes particle physics without spacetime or quantum mechanics as foundations.

hard.q: What is the role of entropy in black hole thermodynamics and the Bekenstein-Hawking formula?
hard.a: Bekenstein proposed black hole entropy is proportional to horizon area (not volume) β€” S = kA/4lpΒ² (Bekenstein-Hawking). This was revolutionary: entropy β area, not volume, suggesting information is encoded on the boundary. This is a foundational insight of the holographic principle and AdS/CFT correspondence.
hard.hint: Black hole entropy scales with surface area, not volume β€” why? This is the key to the holographic principle.

hard.q: What is the Penrose process and how can energy be extracted from a rotating black hole?
hard.a: Rotating (Kerr) black holes have an ergosphere where spacetime is dragged faster than light speed. The Penrose process: a particle enters the ergosphere, splits into two β€” one falls in, one escapes with more energy than the original. Net energy comes from the black hole's rotation. It could theoretically be an energy source.
hard.hint: You can extract energy from a rotating black hole using the ergosphere.

hard.q: What is 'quantum foam' and what physical implications does it have at the Planck scale?
hard.a: At the Planck scale (~10β»Β³βµ m), Heisenberg uncertainty causes space itself to fluctuate wildly β€” quantum foam. Space is not smooth but turbulently uncertain. This implies classical spacetime is only an approximation β€” at the smallest scales, the concept of smooth spacetime breaks down completely.
hard.hint: Below a certain scale, the notion of 'distance' itself becomes undefined.

hard.q: What is the spin-statistics theorem and why does it distinguish fermions from bosons?
hard.a: The spin-statistics theorem (Pauli) connects particle spin to quantum statistics: particles with half-integer spin (fermions) obey Fermi-Dirac statistics (Pauli exclusion principle) β€” no two can be in the same state. Particles with integer spin (bosons) obey Bose-Einstein statistics β€” they prefer the same state. This underlies all of chemistry and materials science.
hard.hint: The difference between matter and light, between electrons and photons, is spin.

hard.q: What is the relationship between quantum field theory and special relativity?
hard.a: Combining QM and special relativity requires quantum field theory (QFT): particles are excitations of underlying fields. This combination predicts antimatter (Dirac equation), vacuum fluctuations, and running coupling constants. The Standard Model is a Lorentz-invariant quantum field theory.
hard.hint: You cannot consistently combine quantum mechanics with special relativity without introducing fields and antimatter.

hard.q: What is the concept of 'effective field theory' and why is it important?
hard.a: Effective field theory (EFT) describes physics at a given energy scale without needing to know the underlying high-energy physics. It captures all relevant degrees of freedom at that scale as an expansion in (E/Ξ›)βΏ where Ξ› is the cutoff. The Standard Model is an EFT β€” valid up to some scale, with unknown physics above.
hard.hint: You don't need to know atomic physics to understand fluid dynamics β€” EFT makes this systematic.

hard.q: What is the connection between the CP violation and the matter-antimatter asymmetry of the universe?
hard.a: CP symmetry (charge conjugation Γ— parity): physical laws should be the same for matter and antimatter. CP violation (small asymmetry in K and B meson decays) shows CP is slightly broken in nature. Sakharov conditions require CP violation for baryogenesis (matter-antimatter asymmetry). But known CP violation is far too small to explain the observed matter-dominated universe.
hard.hint: We know CP is violated β€” but not enough to explain why there's matter at all.

hard.q: What is the landscape problem in string theory?
hard.a: String theory has approximately 10βµβ°β° possible vacuum states (the 'landscape'), each corresponding to a different universe with different physical constants. This makes it enormously difficult to predict which vacuum our universe occupies or to make falsifiable predictions. Some argue it requires anthropic reasoning β€” we live in a vacuum compatible with life.
hard.hint: If there are 10βµβ°β° possible universes, can string theory ever make falsifiable predictions?

hard.q: What is the significance of GΓ¶del's incompleteness theorems for the foundations of physics?
hard.a: GΓ¶del proved formal systems cannot prove all truths about themselves. Some physicists worry this limits physics: could there be true physical statements unprovable from any axiom system? Could a 'theory of everything' be inherently incomplete? Hawking and others have argued GΓ¶del's theorems may impose fundamental limits on physical knowledge.
hard.hint: If mathematics is incomplete, can a mathematical theory of physics be complete?

hard.q: What is decoherence and how does it explain the classical world emerging from quantum mechanics?
hard.a: Quantum superpositions of macroscopic objects are destroyed rapidly by interactions with the environment β€” decoherence. When a quantum system interacts with ~10Β²Β³ environmental particles, superpositions effectively disappear and classical behaviour emerges. Decoherence doesn't fully solve the measurement problem but explains why the classical world doesn't look quantum.
hard.hint: Larger objects interact with more of the environment β€” superpositions are destroyed faster, making the world look classical.

hard.q: What is the relationship between symmetry and conservation laws (Noether's theorem)?
hard.a: Emmy Noether's theorem: every continuous symmetry of a physical system corresponds to a conserved quantity. Time translation symmetry β†’ energy conservation. Spatial translation symmetry β†’ momentum conservation. Rotational symmetry β†’ angular momentum conservation. This is arguably the deepest connection in physics.
hard.hint: Conservation laws are not separate physical facts β€” they all follow from symmetry principles.

hard.q: What are the outstanding problems with the Standard Model beyond the Higgs discovery?
hard.a: SM doesn't include gravity; doesn't explain dark matter or dark energy; doesn't explain matter-antimatter asymmetry; has 19 free parameters that must be measured (not derived); doesn't explain why there are three generations of quarks and leptons; neutrino masses require extensions. Despite success, the SM is clearly incomplete.
hard.hint: The Standard Model is brilliantly successful and obviously incomplete at the same time.

hard.q: What is the significance of gravitational wave detection (LIGO 2015) for physics?
hard.a: LIGO detected gravitational waves from two merging black holes (GW150914, 2015), confirming a prediction of general relativity 100 years after Einstein. It opened gravitational wave astronomy β€” a new way to observe the universe. The 2017 neutron star merger observation also confirmed the r-process (heavy element synthesis) and gamma-ray burst mechanisms.
hard.hint: Einstein predicted gravitational waves in 1916 β€” we confirmed them in 2015.

hard.q: What is quantum biology and what quantum effects have been observed in living systems?
hard.a: Quantum biology studies quantum effects in biological processes. Confirmed examples: photosynthesis uses quantum coherence for near-perfect energy transfer efficiency; DNA mutations can occur via quantum tunnelling (proton transfer); bird navigation may use quantum entanglement in cryptochrome proteins (radical pair mechanism).
hard.hint: Life may have evolved to exploit quantum mechanical effects for efficiency and precision.

hard.q: What is the role of symmetry breaking in the formation of the universe from the Big Bang?
hard.a: As the universe cooled, originally unified forces separated: grand unified theory β†’ strong + electroweak (10β»Β³β¶ s); electroweak β†’ electromagnetic + weak (10β»ΒΉΒ² s, 100 GeV). Each symmetry breaking released energy and produced different particle types. The Higgs mechanism broke the electroweak symmetry, giving W/Z bosons mass.
hard.hint: The early universe was more symmetric β€” today's forces are the result of successive symmetry breakings.

hard.q: What are the philosophical implications of quantum mechanics for determinism and free will?
hard.a: Quantum indeterminacy (Heisenberg) means not all physical outcomes are predetermined. This challenges strict Laplacian determinism (in a deterministic universe, free will is illusory). But quantum indeterminacy doesn't imply free will β€” random outcomes aren't free choices either. Many philosophers argue free will is compatible with determinism anyway.
hard.hint: Does quantum randomness save free will β€” or does it just replace determinism with randomness?

hard.q: What is the concept of 'physical law' and is it descriptive or prescriptive?
hard.a: Physical laws (Newton's laws, Maxwell's equations) are mathematical descriptions of observed regularities. They are descriptive β€” they describe how nature behaves, not prescribe how it must. The question of why nature follows these laws (as opposed to others) is not answered by science β€” it's a philosophical question about the nature of scientific explanation.
hard.hint: Does nature obey the laws of physics, or do we call our best descriptions 'laws' because nature consistently behaves that way?

hard.q: What is the relationship between computational complexity and physical processes?
hard.a: The Church-Turing thesis suggests all physical processes can be simulated by a Turing machine. The physical Church-Turing thesis extends this to quantum processes. If true, no physical process can be more powerful than a quantum computer β€” placing fundamental limits on computation equivalent to limits on physical processes.
hard.hint: Is the universe itself a computer? And if so, what kind?

hard.q: What is the holographic principle and what does it suggest about the fundamental nature of space?
hard.a: The holographic principle (Susskind, Hooft) proposes that the information in a 3D volume of space is fully encoded on its 2D boundary surface β€” like a hologram. This suggests the 3D world we experience may be a projection of a deeper 2D reality. AdS/CFT provides a concrete realisation of this idea.
hard.hint: Our 3D universe might be the 'shadow' of a 2D quantum field theory.

hard.q: What are the theoretical limits of human knowledge according to physics and mathematics?
hard.a: Physical limits: Planck scale (below which classical spacetime breaks down); cosmological horizon (can't observe beyond); quantum uncertainty (can't simultaneously know position and momentum precisely). Mathematical limits: GΓ¶del's incompleteness; Turing's undecidability. Together, they suggest that complete knowledge of reality may be fundamentally impossible.
hard.hint: Both physics and mathematics have built-in limits on what can be known.

easy.q: What is the difference between synchronic and diachronic linguistics?
easy.a: Synchronic linguistics studies a language at a single point in time. Diachronic (historical) linguistics studies language change over time.
easy.hint: Sync = at the same time; dia = through time.

easy.q: What is a morpheme?
easy.a: The smallest meaningful unit of language. 'Unhappiness' has three morphemes: un- (not), happy (base), -ness (state of being)
easy.hint: Morphemes can be words or parts of words (prefixes, suffixes).

easy.q: What is the difference between prescriptive and descriptive grammar?
easy.a: Prescriptive grammar sets rules for 'correct' language use. Descriptive grammar describes how people actually use language, without judgment of correctness.
easy.hint: Linguists are descriptivists; school grammar books are prescriptivists.

easy.q: What is code-switching in linguistics?
easy.a: The practice of alternating between two or more languages or dialects in a single conversation or utterance
easy.hint: Bilingual speakers often code-switch naturally.

easy.q: What is the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis?
easy.a: The hypothesis that the language you speak shapes the way you think and perceive the world (linguistic relativity / linguistic determinism)
easy.hint: Does language determine thought, or just influence it?

easy.q: What is a 'speech act' (Austin)?
easy.a: A speech act is an utterance that performs an action rather than just describing: promises, orders, apologies, declarations. Austin distinguished locutionary act (saying), illocutionary act (performing), and perlocutionary act (effect on hearer).
easy.hint: 'I promise' doesn't describe a promise β€” it performs one.

easy.q: What is a paradox in literature?
easy.a: A statement that seems self-contradictory but contains a deeper truth (e.g., 'Less is more', 'The more I learn, the less I know')
easy.hint: It seems impossible but illuminates something real.

easy.q: What is a solecism?
easy.a: A grammatical mistake or violation of the rules of language use
easy.hint: 'I have went' instead of 'I have gone' is a solecism.

easy.q: What is anachronism in literature or film?
easy.a: Something that is historically out of place β€” appearing in a time period when it did not exist (e.g., a wristwatch in a film set in ancient Rome)
easy.hint: Ana = against; chronos = time.

easy.q: What is the distinction between 'story' and 'narrative' in literary theory?
easy.a: Story (fabula): the events in their chronological order as they occurred. Narrative (sjuzhet): how those events are arranged, presented, and told β€” which may be non-linear, selective, or framed.
easy.hint: The same story can be told with many different narratives.

easy.q: What is a 'motif' versus a 'symbol' in literature?
easy.a: A symbol carries a specific meaning beyond itself (a dove = peace). A motif is a recurring element (image, idea, phrase) throughout a work that contributes to theme without necessarily having a fixed symbolic meaning.
easy.hint: Symbols stand for something specific; motifs create patterns.

easy.q: What is the 'fourth wall'?
easy.a: The imaginary wall between the fictional world and the audience. Breaking the fourth wall means a character directly addresses the audience or acknowledges being in a story.
easy.hint: Deadpool constantly breaks the fourth wall.

easy.q: What is a 'foil' character?
easy.a: A character whose contrasting qualities highlight the protagonist's characteristics (e.g., Mercutio's flamboyance highlights Romeo's romantic intensity)
easy.hint: The foil makes the protagonist's qualities more visible by contrast.

easy.q: What is 'bathos'?
easy.a: An abrupt descent from the elevated to the trivial, creating comic or deflating effect (e.g., 'She was beautiful, intelligent, courageous β€” and always left the toilet seat up')
easy.hint: A sudden anticlimax β€” the contrast creates the effect.

easy.q: What is the difference between deductive and inductive writing structures?
easy.a: Deductive: begins with a general claim (thesis) then provides evidence. Inductive: begins with specific evidence then builds to a general conclusion.
easy.hint: Top-down (deductive) vs. bottom-up (inductive).

easy.q: What is a 'coda' in narrative structure?
easy.a: A brief concluding section that follows the main resolution, providing final information about characters or events after the climax β€” a final reflection or postscript
easy.hint: Often addresses what happened 'afterwards.'

easy.q: What is 'catharsis' in Aristotle's Poetics?
easy.a: The emotional purging experienced by an audience watching tragedy β€” through pity and fear, accumulated emotional tension is released, leaving the audience cleansed and satisfied
easy.hint: Aristotle saw tragedy as emotionally therapeutic.

easy.q: What is an 'unreliable setting' in fiction?
easy.a: A setting that cannot be fully trusted or is ambiguously real β€” the physical world reflects or distorts the narrator's unreliable perception (e.g., Poe's stories where the setting mirrors the narrator's madness)
easy.hint: When the setting can't be trusted, neither can the narrator's perception.

easy.q: What is 'polyphony' in a novel (Bakhtin)?
easy.a: A narrative where multiple voices coexist with equal weight and authority, without one dominating perspective β€” the author doesn't impose a single viewpoint, each character speaks for themselves
easy.hint: Dostoevsky's novels are the classic examples.

easy.q: What is an 'elegy' and what distinguishes it from other poetic forms?
easy.a: An elegy mourns the dead or reflects on loss β€” typically moving through grief to acceptance or consolation. Tone: mournful but often ending with some peace or transcendence.
easy.hint: Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' is the classic English example.

easy.q: What is the difference between a 'lyric' and an 'epic' in classical terms?
easy.a: Lyric poetry: short, expressive of personal emotion, first person (odes, sonnets, elegies). Epic poetry: long narrative poem concerning heroic deeds, usually third person, elevated diction (Iliad, Aeneid, Paradise Lost).
easy.hint: Lyric = personal feeling; epic = heroic narrative.

easy.q: What is a 'round' versus a 'flat' character (E.M. Forster)?
easy.a: Flat characters are defined by a single trait and don't change. Round characters are complex, multi-dimensional, and capable of surprising the reader in a convincing way.
easy.hint: Forster: flat characters can be summed up in a sentence; round characters cannot.

easy.q: What is 'in medias res' and why is it used?
easy.a: Starting a narrative in the middle of the action, rather than at the chronological beginning. Effect: immediate excitement, in-the-action feel, motivates reader curiosity about prior events.
easy.hint: The Iliad begins in the tenth year of the Trojan War, not at its start.

easy.q: What is the difference between 'theme' and 'subject' in literature?
easy.a: Subject is what a text is about (e.g., war). Theme is what the text says about that subject β€” the underlying idea or argument (e.g., 'War dehumanises those who wage it').
easy.hint: Subject = topic. Theme = message about that topic.

easy.q: What is 'metonymy'?
easy.a: A figure of speech where something is referred to by a closely related aspect of it (e.g., 'The Crown' referring to the monarchy; 'the pen is mightier than the sword' β€” pen=writing, sword=military force)
easy.hint: Not literally the same thing, but closely associated.

easy.q: What is 'synecdoche'?
easy.a: A figure of speech where a part represents the whole (or vice versa). 'All hands on deck' (hands = sailors). 'The US won gold' (the US = the specific athlete).
easy.hint: Part for whole, or whole for part.

easy.q: What is the 'pathetic fallacy'?
easy.a: Attributing human emotions to the natural world or inanimate objects (e.g., 'the angry storm', 'the weeping skies'). Often used to reflect a character's emotional state.
easy.hint: Ruskin coined the term. It's a specific type of personification related to the natural world.

easy.q: What is a 'stream of consciousness' narrative?
easy.a: A narrative technique representing the continuous, unfiltered flow of a character's thoughts, impressions, and feelings β€” often without conventional punctuation or chronological order
easy.hint: Virginia Woolf and James Joyce pioneered this technique.

easy.q: What is 'negative capability' (Keats)?
easy.a: Keats described negative capability as the capacity to remain in uncertainty and doubt without irritably grasping after reason and fact. He considered it essential for creative and poetic thinking.
easy.hint: Great art tolerates ambiguity without forcing resolution.

easy.q: What is the 'willing suspension of disbelief' (Coleridge)?
easy.a: The reader voluntarily accepts fictional elements as real within the story's world, enabling engagement with obviously impossible events or settings
easy.hint: You know Hogwarts isn't real β€” but you accept it as real while reading.

easy.q: What is the difference between a 'narrator' and a 'focaliser' (Genette)?
easy.a: The narrator is who tells the story. The focaliser is who sees or perceives the events (whose perspective we inhabit). These can be different: an omniscient narrator might focalise through a character's limited perspective.
easy.hint: Who speaks vs. who sees β€” they need not be the same.

easy.q: What is an 'apostrophe' as a literary device?
easy.a: Addressing an absent person, abstract concept, or inanimate object as if it were present and could respond (e.g., 'O death, where is thy sting?'; 'O liberty, what crimes are committed in thy name!')
easy.hint: Not a punctuation mark here β€” a direct address to something that cannot reply.

easy.q: What is 'parataxis' in literature?
easy.a: The placing of clauses or phrases one after another without conjunctions or subordination, often creating a staccato or matter-of-fact effect (e.g., 'I came. I saw. I conquered.')
easy.hint: Opposite of hypotaxis (complex subordination). Think Hemingway's direct style.

easy.q: What is 'ekphrasis' in literature?
easy.a: A vivid verbal description of a visual work of art (painting, sculpture, tapestry), often functioning to pause the narrative and allow contemplation. Famous example: Keats's 'Ode on a Grecian Urn.'
easy.hint: The poem about the painting about the story β€” art describing art.

easy.q: What is the 'implied author' (Wayne Booth)?
easy.a: The sense of the author constructed from the values and choices embedded in the text β€” distinct from both the real author and the narrator. Allows critics to discuss authorial values without making biographical claims.
easy.hint: The author we construct from reading the text is not necessarily the real person.

easy.q: What is 'fabula' and 'syuzhet' in Russian Formalist narratology?
easy.a: Fabula: the chronological sequence of story events as they happened. Syuzhet: the arrangement of those events in the narrative β€” which may be non-linear, framed, or selective. Syuzhet is what the reader encounters; fabula is what must be inferred.
easy.hint: Fabula is the 'what'; syuzhet is the 'how of the telling.'

easy.q: What is 'tautology' in logic and rhetoric?
easy.a: In logic: a statement that is necessarily true by virtue of its form (e.g., 'it will either rain or it won't'). In rhetoric: unnecessary repetition of an idea (e.g., 'free gift').
easy.hint: In logic it's always true; in rhetoric it's redundant.

easy.q: What is 'anadiplosis'?
easy.a: A rhetorical device repeating the last word of one clause as the first word of the next (e.g., 'Fear leads to anger. Anger leads to hatred. Hatred leads to suffering.' β€” Yoda)
easy.hint: The word bridges the gap between clauses.

easy.q: What is 'circumlocution'?
easy.a: The use of many words where few would do β€” going around a point rather than stating it directly. Can be used for comic effect, to soften something, or as a rhetorical strategy.
easy.hint: Speaking in circles rather than coming to the point.

easy.q: What is the difference between 'denotation', 'connotation', and 'implicature'?
easy.a: Denotation: literal meaning. Connotation: emotional/cultural associations. Implicature (Grice): what is implied or communicated beyond what is literally said, based on conversational conventions.
easy.hint: 'Can you pass the salt?' literally asks about ability; it implies a request.

easy.q: What is a 'dramatic monologue'?
easy.a: A poem in which a single speaker addresses a silent listener, often revealing the speaker's character through what they say and don't say. Famous examples: Browning's 'My Last Duchess.'
easy.hint: The speaker reveals more than they intend β€” often ironically.

easy.q: What is 'intersubjectivity' in the context of communication?
easy.a: The shared meanings, understandings, and assumptions between people in communication β€” the common ground that makes meaning possible. Without intersubjectivity, communication would be impossible.
easy.hint: We can communicate because we share frameworks of meaning.

easy.q: What is the concept of 'defamiliarisation' (Shklovsky) and how is it related to art's social function?
easy.a: Defamiliarisation (ostranenie) makes the familiar strange, forcing us to perceive things anew rather than automatically. Art's function: to counteract the automatisation of perception that makes us see the world without really seeing it.
easy.hint: Literature forces you to see the familiar world as if for the first time.

easy.q: What is a 'KΓΌnstlerroman'?
easy.a: A novel about an artist's development β€” a subtype of the Bildungsroman focusing specifically on the formation of artistic identity and the conflict between the artist and society. Example: Joyce's A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.
easy.hint: KΓΌnstler = artist in German. An artist's coming-of-age.

easy.q: What is the concept of 'negative space' in literary composition?
